newsitem.title: UK: Passenger services resume through Channel Tunnel.
newsitem.headline: Passenger services resume through Channel Tunnel.

text.p: Passenger trains resumed services through the fire-damaged Anglo-French Channel tunnel early on Wednesday, tunnel operator Eurotunnel said.
Only a few passengers boarded the first few trains to leave London's Waterloo station for Paris and Brussels, said Eurostar, which runs the express passenger trains.
It said it planned to resume 90 percent of its normal services. A spokesman said it would run 13 trains a day to Paris and seven to Brussels.
The tunnel has been closed to all passenger traffic since November 18, when a fire on a truck destroyed a freight shuttle train and severely damaged a section of the tunnel, injuring 34 people.
Eurotunnel staged a drill on Sunday to show it could safely run passenger services when one of the two rail tunnels is still closed for repairs.

Late on Tuesday the the Inter-Governmental Commission (IGC) of French and British government representatives said it had accepted the advice of its safety committee that a limited service could resume while repairs continued.
But Ken Cameron of Britain's Fire Brigades Union said he had serious questions about the tunnel's safety.

"Here we are within two weeks of a major fire, where we have got a construction site operating in the tunnel, which is going to cause tremendous problems of congestion, or of the the accidents that do happen on building sites," he told BBC radio.

Cameron said an escape tunnel meant for evacuating passengers was still damaged and said Sunday's drill had not reassured him. "I think that was an absolute exercise in public relations rather than safety," he said.

"The fact that the train didn't uncouple, the fact that evacuation of smoke did not take place, the fact that the train was not able to carry on out of the tunnel -- all of these things have not been answered, yet we're putting Eurostar down there today with hundreds of people on board."
Adam Mills, executive deputy chairman of Eurostar, said the company had been assured the tunnel was safe.
"We certainly would never do anything which would prejudice the safety of our Eurostar passengers," he told BBC.

"We are satisfied that we are operating our Eurostar trains to the standards of safety which we always have done. And we have also received the assurances that the tunnel, in operational mode, is as it has been for our purposes."
Eurostar said journeys to Paris would take half and hour longer than usual, while those to Brussels would take 45 minutes longer.
Eurostar, a joint venture between Eurostar UK and the French and Belgian national railways, had been running up to 24 return services a day from London to Paris and Brussels before the fire.

The first Paris-bound train left London's Waterloo station at 0550 GMT with only crew, journalists and a public relations officer aboard, but two fare-paying passengers joined the train at Ashford in Kent. Later trains had a scattering of pasengers.
Debt-laden Eurotunnel will restart its Le Shuttle passenger vehicle services from December 10. ($1=.5995 Pound)
